title: Satluj Review: Diljit Dosanjh Delivers a Career-Defining Performance in Banned Punjab Drama
excerpt: Honey Trehan's biographical film about human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra drew 6.58 million views in 48 hours before being pulled from ZEE5 in India. International audiences are driving a 374% surge in app downloads.
body:
• Diljit Dosanjh delivers what critics are calling a career-defining performance as human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra, who exposed thousands of extrajudicial killings in 1990s Punjab.
  • The film drew 6.58 million views on ZEE5 in 48 hours before being removed in India, sparking a censorship debate and a 374% surge in international app downloads.
  • After a four-year battle with the censor board involving 127 demanded cuts and three title changes, Satluj has become a flashpoint for free expression in Indian cinema.

A Film That Refused to Be Silenced

Satluj is not a comfortable film, and it was never intended to be one. Directed by Honey Trehan and released on ZEE5 on July 3 without prior marketing, this biographical drama about Jaswant Singh Khalra — a bank manager who uncovered evidence of thousands of extrajudicial cremations by Punjab Police in the 1990s — arrived with the weight of a story that powerful institutions have spent decades trying to bury.

Within 48 hours, it had been watched 6.58 million times. Then the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting ordered ZEE5 to take it down in India, citing national security concerns. By July 11, even international viewers lost access. The ban has done what bans often do: amplified the conversation.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Xei8D-j8dx8

"Just saw SATLUJ and it is not a film, but a deep wound that will never heal. It stirs up the sludge in one of the darkest chapters of our history. This is cinema used as confrontation."

— Ram Gopal Varma, filmmaker

A Slow-Burn Investigation, Not a Hero's Arc

Trehan wisely avoids the temptation of turning Khalra into a larger-than-life figure. Rather than presenting a conventional biopic, the film unfolds as a slow-burning investigative thriller set during Punjab's turbulent insurgency years. Diljit Dosanjh, who reportedly charged a symbolic ₹1 to play the role, inhabits Khalra with a quiet fury that builds through restraint rather than spectacle.

The narrative is framed through the CBI investigation that followed Khalra's disappearance, led by Additional Director Samudra Singh, played with measured authority by Arjun Rampal. Suvinder Vicky delivers a chilling turn as SSP Surjit Singh Sugga, while Kanwaljit Singh's portrayal of a DGP navigating institutional complicity adds another layer of moral complexity.

Geetika Vidya Ohlyan is excellent as Paramjit, Khalra's wife, capturing the fear and resilience of someone watching a loved one place principle above personal safety. Saurabh Sachdeva's performance as Satnam Singh, a constable torn between loyalty and conscience, demonstrates that humanity can survive even within deeply compromised systems.

Critical Acclaim Across the Board

The critical consensus has been overwhelmingly positive. Filmfare gave it 4 out of 5 stars, calling it "a film that educates, disturbs and moves in equal measure." NDTV's Saibal Chatterjee awarded 4 stars, describing it as "a powerful political film that pulls no punches." The Indian Express rated it 3.5 stars, with Shubhra Gupta noting there is "nothing generic about the film" and calling it "a clear win for filmmakers who want to tell the story of an actual person, time and place, with unwavering conviction."

The Hollywood Reporter India called it "Hearty and Harrowing" and one of the finest Indian films of the year. The Hindu praised Dosanjh as "a solitary lamp whose conviction outlasts the darkest night." Even reviewers who found the 163-minute runtime occasionally indulgent acknowledged the film's power and relevance.

The Censorship Battle

The film's production history is itself a story of institutional resistance. Originally titled Ghallughara, it was completed in 2022 but faced demands for 127 cuts from the Central Board of Film Certification. The filmmakers changed the title to Punjab '95, then to Satluj, each time attempting to navigate the regulatory obstacle course. A planned premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival was pulled. Private screenings were reportedly blocked. Director Trehan told New Lines Magazine that he was "called by the people in power to stop the screening."

The uncut version finally reached audiences through ZEE5's quiet July 3 release — a guerrilla approach that Dosanjh himself anticipated would be short-lived. "It can happen," he told fans on Instagram Live. "There's that fear. But let's worry not. Those who want to stop the film can do that."

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For the Punjabi diaspora in the US, Canada, and the UK, Satluj has become more than a film — it is a reckoning with a chapter of history that many families carry in their bones. ZEE5 Global saw a 374% surge in international app downloads following the Indian ban, reflecting the depth of engagement from overseas audiences. The story of Khalra, who disappeared in 1995 and whose body was never recovered, resonates with communities that include survivors and descendants of the insurgency era.

Produced by Ronnie Screwvala and Abhishek Chaubey on a reported budget of $4.5 million, Satluj stands as proof that some stories refuse to be silenced — and that the attempt to silence them only makes them louder.
